title: The Shape of an Agreement
subtitle: Lanternweald — sixth expansion pass
content:
The calendar had survived salt spray, one dropped kettle, and three months of Maui writing appointments in letters large enough to be seen from the harbor. It did not survive his attempt to improve it.

I found it on the kitchen table with a line drawn through Thursday.

Thursday had been ours.

He had replaced it with a note: *Helping Fen. Necessary.*

I stood there holding a parcel from Moonroot Archive, still wearing the coat I'd put on that morning to come home early. We'd planned the evening two weeks ago. Not a festival, not a rescue, not a shift at the pantry. Dinner, the little blue blanket, and absolutely no public meetings.

"Maui?"

He came in carrying a coil of rope. "Before you say anything, the new mooring—"

"You canceled our evening."

He looked at the calendar. "Moved it. Friday's open."

"Friday Iroh and I are reviewing the terrace map."

"Then Saturday."

"Saturday you promised Lio you'd inspect the skiff."

His smile faltered. "Right."

I set the parcel beside the stove. The air smelled like wet rope and rosemary. I wanted to say something spectacularly unfair, something about being last on his list. A familiar, uglier part of me wanted to win the argument before he knew it had begun.

Instead I said, "You didn't ask me."

Maui put down the rope. "Fen needed someone to help secure the landing before the wind shifts."

"Fen could need help. I might even agree that it's urgent. Neither changes the fact that you decided what happened to my evening without telling me."

"I thought you'd understand."

"I do understand the mooring. I don't understand why you didn't send a note."

He rubbed his face. "I was busy."

"So busy you had time to rewrite the calendar."

That landed.

He looked at the enormous letters he'd written across Thursday. "Okay. That was bad."

I pulled out a chair. "Sit with me?"

He sat, awkwardly. His injured hand had healed, but he still curled his fingers when he was ashamed, as if bracing for a blow that wasn't coming.

"I made a mistake," he said. "I should have asked."

"Thank you."

"I need to know something, too."

I waited.

"Sometimes I look at that calendar and feel like I'm asking for an appointment with someone who has six lives. Then I hate myself for thinking it, because you told me from the beginning that you're ethically non-monogamous and prefer polyamory. I agreed to that knowing what it meant."

"I don't have six lives," I said. "I have one. It's the same me coming to your door."

"I know."

"Knowing doesn't mean you stop feeling lonely."

He looked at me, surprised.

I turned the calendar around. Its edges were curled. Under my appointments he'd added tiny drawings of fish and hooks. Beneath my private time with Severus, he'd written *No questions*. He had been trying, in his own untidy way, to respect agreements he didn't always find easy.

"Can we write down what we actually mean?" I asked.

"Without making it a contract that gets me arrested?"

"Preferably."

We took a clean sheet from the green notebook. Across the top I wrote *Our present agreements—not ownership, not forever.*

Maui leaned over to read it.

"That's a long title."

"We can edit."

We agreed to tell each other about schedule changes before altering shared plans, unless there was an immediate emergency. In that case we would send word as soon as safely possible. We agreed not to share details about my other partners' private lives without their permission. He could ask for reassurance, and I could answer honestly without ranking anybody.

Most importantly, either of us could say no to a date, a conversation, a kiss, or a request for time. No explanation was required to make a no count.

Maui studied the last line.

"If you say no because you need quiet, can I ask when we might talk again?"

"Yes. That's a request, not a demand. Sometimes I won't know."

He nodded.

"And if I need quiet?"

"Then you get it too."

We left space at the bottom to revise the page. We signed it with our names, not as a legal instrument but because the act made us both laugh. Maui drew a small fish beside his signature. Its expression was deeply suspicious.

I glanced at the clock.

"You still have the mooring shift?"

"Yes. Fen's expecting me."

"Then go. I don't want the landing to fail because we were arguing."

He paused at the door. "Are we all right?"

"We're working on it."

He seemed to take that more seriously than any grand assurance I could have given.

The next morning he sent a message before the agreed hour. Fen's inspection had uncovered a worn ring. They would need another half-day, and he wanted to know whether I minded moving our meal to Sunday.

I smiled at the message.

*Sunday works. Ask Lio whether Saturday still suits them.*

He answered with a picture of a fish whose fins were holding a calendar.

On Sunday, we made dinner together. Maui burned the first flatbread. I misread the spice jar and filled the kitchen with cinnamon. We ate the second batch outside by the sheltered garden, where the sea kale was growing slowly but stubbornly.

"Can I kiss you?" he asked when we'd cleared the plates.

"Yes."

His thumb brushed my cheek. He kissed me as though he didn't want the moment to finish, then drew back to ask whether I was cold.

"A little," I admitted.

He fetched the blue blanket.

We sat close, the sea breathing beyond the stones, and I let my head rest against him. Later we closed our door and kept the evening to ourselves.

In the morning the calendar was still hanging. Thursday was crossed out, Sunday carried a small blue star, and our new agreement lay beside the green notebook, ready to be revised when life made more honesty necessary.

It was paper.

We were the people who had to keep choosing what it meant.
